title: A regulatory badge. A very different reality.
subject: speedysure.co.uk
summary: An insurance site claims FCA regulation. The regulator identifies it as a clone firm.
lesson: Verify a regulatory claim with the regulator, using contact details from its official register.
image_alt: Archived SpeedySure website offering car insurance from £4.50 an hour and claiming FCA regulation.
observations: A prominent badge claims FCA regulation.
A low hourly price, customer count and instant-quote buttons encourage registration.
The capture presents the service as an established insurance provider.
source_summary: The FCA names SpeedySure and speedysure.co.uk in a clone-firm warning. Desenmascara separately records a Suspicious assessment of 60/100 in report #11454.
limits: The image is a historical capture; its exact capture date is not established here. The source assessments are attributed separately. The screenshot does not establish AI use or customer losses. The genuine firm named by the FCA is separate from the clone.

title: A global operation. An identity still to verify.
subject: folonicalogistics.com
summary: A cargo-port image, certification claim and parcel tracker present the appearance of an established carrier.
lesson: A transport website does not establish that a carrier exists. Verify the company identity and any certification through independent records before entrusting it with money or goods.
image_alt: Archived Folanica-branded logistics page with container ships, port cranes, a certification claim and yellow Track Parcel buttons.
observations: A large photograph of container ships and port cranes suggests an international shipping operation.
A certification badge makes an authority claim without identifying a certifier in this captured view.
Parcel-tracking buttons and service navigation make the page look operational; the image cannot show whether those services work.
source_summary: Desenmascara report #152096 records a Fraudulent assessment of 95/100, attributed to a PhishDestroy DestroyList match. Its accompanying analysis says the operator’s legal identity could not be verified and flags a recently registered domain.
limits: This is a suspected ghost-company facade, not an independent finding that no registered company exists. The historical capture does not establish ownership of the pictured ships, a working tracking system, customer losses or a payment demand. Its capture date is unknown. The report also labels text as AI-generated, but that automated attribution is not proof of authorship. Shared hosting or a young domain alone does not prove fraud.

title: A famous face. An unverified promise.
subject: Sanewex · domain partially masked in source
summary: Celebrity imagery and supposed official partnerships make a crypto casino look credible.
lesson: A famous face or familiar logo is a website’s claim. Check endorsements through the supposed partner’s own channels.
image_alt: Archived Sanewex casino page displaying Elon Musk and X and SpaceX partnership claims.
observations: Elon Musk’s image appears beside a claim that he backs the casino.
X and SpaceX branding is labeled as an official partnership.
A bonus invitation sits alongside large player and payout figures.
source_summary: Desenmascara classifies the page as a crypto gambling scam involving celebrity impersonation. Its rationale cites unverified partnership claims and no visible legitimate licensing information.
limits: This is Desenmascara’s recorded assessment, not a new investigation. The screenshot does not establish that AI created the page or images, or that the displayed payout figures are real. Follow the original report for context and corrections.

title: Your earnings are ready. First, send money.
subject: Task scam pattern
summary: A supposed job shows earnings, then demands a deposit before you can withdraw them.
lesson: A number on a dashboard does not prove that withdrawable earnings exist. Do not send money to release supposed wages.
message: Great work! Your task balance is now €184. To withdraw it, top up your account with €60 to complete the final task set. The deposit will be returned with your earnings.
observations: An apparent job offers commissions for simple online tasks.
A displayed balance makes the earnings feel real.
A separate payment is demanded before those supposed earnings can be withdrawn.
source_summary: FTC guidance describes task scams in which an online platform displays apparent commissions, then asks the person to deposit their own money. The message here is an educational reconstruction of that pattern.
limits: The wording and amounts are invented. This is not a victim’s message or an accusation against a named business. A legitimate payout minimum is different from asking someone to send a separate deposit. AI involvement is not established.
audience: Job seekers and online task workers

observations: A Spanish storefront advertises large discounts and daily offers.
Cart and account controls make the page look like a conventional shop.
The screenshot does not identify who ultimately receives a buyer’s payment.

limits: Shared hosting is not proof of common ownership or fraud. The screenshot cannot establish non-delivery, stolen payments or AI-generated content. The classification belongs to the source; this card adds no independent verdict.

title: A lawful-looking request. A disclosure to the wrong party.
audience: Banks, fintechs, legal and compliance teams; affected customers as data subjects
subject: Revolut customer-data disclosure after fraudulent government-domain requests
summary: Revolut confirmed that sensitive customer data was disclosed after fraudulent information requests were sent from a legitimate government-agency email domain.
lesson: For regulated firms, a trusted domain is not enough. Sensitive data requests need independent requester verification, authority checks and escalation paths before records leave the institution.
counterclaim: Requester authority must be independently verified
observations: The reported attack targeted a compliance workflow rather than a public scam landing page.
Revolut told TechCrunch the requests came from a legitimate government-agency email domain and were fraudulent.
Reportedly exposed data included identity and contact details, identity-document copies, and possibly selfies, statements and transaction histories.
Revolut said its systems and customer funds were unaffected, while affected customers were contacted directly.
source_summary: TechCrunch reported on 12 September 2026 that Revolut confirmed a limited number of customers were impacted after fraudulent information requests were sent from a legitimate government-agency email domain. The Block separately reported that the incident involved KYC and account data, with possible Bitcoin transaction history exposure. The Financial Times later reported that nearly 700 customers were affected and that the UK Information Commissioner's Office had opened an investigation.
limits: This case is based on public reporting and Revolut statements quoted by those outlets. The government agency, exact request documents, affected markets and final regulator findings were not publicly established in these sources. The incident should not be described as customer funds being stolen or Revolut's core systems being compromised unless later evidence supports that.
assessment_source: TechCrunch, The Block and Financial Times
